Q: Unable to torch.load due to pickling/safety error A:

I see two main issues here:

  1. The checkpoint that you are trying to load contains instances of NumPy 1.x classes/functions, while you are trying to load it in an environment with NumPy 2.x.
  2. The checkpoint that you are trying to load contains an actual model rather than model weights only.

As to 1 (NumPy version)

A lot of changes, some of them breaking changes, happened in the step from NumPy 1.x to NumPy 2.x, one of them being privatizing the numpy.core namespace. That is, classes that could be found under numpy.core in NumPy 1.x are now under numpy._core. The error message that you get is admittedly not that helpful in this context.

Luckily, add_safe_globals() and safe_globals() provide a mechanism to handle situations like this, in that both enable providing explicitly the connection between the place and name of a serialized (pickled) component at serialization time and at deserialization time (emphasis by me):

Each item in the list [of safe_globals, that is to say] can either be a function/class or a tuple of the form (function/class, string) where string is the full path of the function/class.

Here, we can use function/class to refer to the new location (_core in the given case) and name, while string may refer to the old location (core in the given case) and name of the function/class of interest.

The particular problem described in the question can be fixed with

import numpy as np
...

with torch.serialization.safe_globals([
        (np._core.multiarray._reconstruct, "numpy.core.multiarray._reconstruct")
    ]):
    ...

in a Python environment with NumPy 2.x.

As to 2 (model vs. model weights)

It seems like someone stored a complete model instance as part of their checkpoint (torch.save({"model": model, …}, …)) rather than the model weights only (torch.save({"model": model.state_dict(), …}, …). As a consequence, rather than only loading PyTorch tensors and scalars, which are considered safe by default, we have to allow all components that are used in the model itself (e.g. torch.nn.modules.batchnorm.BatchNorm2d or models.yolo.Model) via add_safe_globals()/safe_globals().

Putting it all together

I was able to load the checkpoint of the given file with the following code:

import os, numpy as np, torch
from yolov5 import models

checkpoint_path = os.path.expanduser("~/Downloads/signatureyolo.pt")  # TODO: Adjust

with torch.serialization.safe_globals([
        (np._core.multiarray._reconstruct, "numpy.core.multiarray._reconstruct"),
        np.ndarray,
        np.dtype,
        np.dtypes.Float64DType,
        torch.nn.modules.container.Sequential,
        torch.nn.modules.container.ModuleList,
        torch.nn.modules.conv.Conv2d,
        torch.nn.modules.batchnorm.BatchNorm2d,
        torch.nn.modules.activation.SiLU,
        torch.nn.modules.pooling.MaxPool2d,
        torch.nn.modules.upsampling.Upsample,
        (models.yolo.DetectionModel, "models.yolo.Model"),
        (models.yolo.Detect, "models.yolo.Detect"),
        (models.common.Focus, "models.common.Focus"),
        (models.common.Conv, "models.common.Conv"),
        (models.common.C3, "models.common.C3"),
        (models.common.Bottleneck, "models.common.Bottleneck"),
        (models.common.SPP, "models.common.SPP"),
        (models.common.Concat, "models.common.Concat"),
    ]):
    ckpt = torch.load(checkpoint_path, weights_only=True, map_location="cpu")

print(ckpt)
# {'epoch': -1, 'best_fitness': array([    0.49472]), 'training_results': None, 'model': DetectionModel(
#   (model): Sequential(
#     (0): Focus(
#       (conv): Conv(
#         (conv): Conv2d(12, 80, kernel_size=(3, 3), stride=(1, 1), padding=(1, 1), bias=False)
#         (bn): BatchNorm2d(80, eps=0.001, momentum=0.03, affine=True, track_running_stats=True)
#         (act): SiLU()
# ...

I am not entirely sure why I needed the tuple approach for the models.common and models.yolo components, since, except for the first one, both elements in each tuple match exactly. I assume that it's again a location problem (yolov5.models.* vs. models.* here, so with vs. without yolov5 prefix – note the from yolov5 import models import in this context), but I didn't dig any further. In any case, I couldn't get it to work without using explicit strings here, as well.

The relevant parts of my environment:

  • Python 3.13.9
  • PyTorch 2.10.0
  • NumPy 2.4.1
  • YOLOv5 7.0.14

Avoiding the problem

To get rid of the hassle in the future, I would suggest saving your own version of the checkpoint, ensuring that only native Python classes and PyTorch tensors are contained. So, in particular:

  • use native Python scalars, or maybe PyTorch tensors rather than NumPy scalars or arrays (e.g. use a native python float rather than a 1-element NumPy array for the checkpoint's "best_fitness" entry);
  • use model.state_dict() rather than model (e.g. for the checkpoint's "model" entry).

You are actually still lucky here that, at the time of writing this, the checkpoint can still be loaded, even with newer package versions, in the first place. This is because all stored components are still available and compatible, albeit partially under different names and places. Once these components themselves change (such as, dropping old or adopting new class fields – see this answer to a related question), you might be out of luck even with the solution (or rather, workaround) described under Putting it all together above.

Note that this is not specifically a PyTorch problem, not even a Python problem, but a problem of serializing/deserializing programmatic content in general. And this is why the approach of saving only Python scalars and PyTorch tensors suggested above is most promising in my opinion: While these components may also evolve over time, they are evolved with serialization compatibility in mind, while other components might not be.

Q: Check if current .NET version is still supported in C# A:

The .NET 4.5 version are from 2021 and earlier. I will not touch these versions if not needed.

Yes, the problem is the software or company policy. As long as the software is in use, I have to support it. The responsible persons are free to update to the new versions. The only problem is that the update means a lot of effort as my program is only a small component of a big software solution. This is the reason why some people don't update.

The check of the .NET version should just be an additional argument for an update.
